scope: AQA 7357 FIRST school mock: Year 1 Pure only (no Statistics, Mechanics, Year 2 or radians); targeted application evidence for selected previously documented weak areas.
method: Match each selected original v334 skill code to its exact original, loaded, mock-eligible AS Pure multi-mark practice question ID; preserve actual question prompt and marks. A practice question being present does not mean student working or alternative grading is certified.

rows.originalSkill: Proof by deduction: consecutive integers and divisibility
rows.note: Full deduction for divisibility claims, not just stating a proof method.

linkedPractice.prompt: Let n be any integer. Prove by deduction that n³ − n is divisible by 6.
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

linkedPractice.prompt: For an arbitrary integer n, prove by deduction that n⁴ − n² is divisible by 12. Your proof must explain divisibility by 3 and 4, considering the necessary integer cases. [6 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.originalSkill: Proof by exhaustion and finite-domain completeness
rows.note: Show exhaustive enumeration and justify finite-domain completeness.

linkedPractice.prompt: The integer n is restricted to −2 ≤ n ≤ 3. Prove by exhaustion that n² + 3n + 2 is even for every allowed n. Make the finite domain explicit. [4 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.note: Check interval signs, inclusion of zero numerator and exclusion of zero denominators; the older v334 crosswalk lacked links.

linkedPractice.prompt: Solve (x² − x − 6)/(x − 1) ≤ 0. Show the critical values, justify the signs of the expression in each interval, and state the solution using inequalities or interval notation. [7 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

linkedPractice.prompt: Solve (x² − x − 2)/(x² − 6x + 8) ≤ 0. Explain why cancelling a common factor does not make every value of x valid. Give your final solution as intervals. [7 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.note: Reciprocal graph asymptote transformations and valid x domain require actual sketches.

linkedPractice.prompt: The curve is y=f(x)=1/x. Sketch y=g(x)=f(x−2)+3. Clearly show and label both asymptotes, the transformed points corresponding to (1,1) and (−1,−1), the x-intercept and the y-intercept. [6 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

linkedPractice.prompt: Start with f(x)=1/x². Sketch y=g(x)=3f(x+1)−2. Label both asymptotes, the transformed points corresponding to (−1,1) and (1,1), the y-intercept and the two exact x-intercepts. Show both branches clearly. [6 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.originalSkill: Algebraic fractions and forbidden denominator inputs
rows.note: Cancelling factors never restores an originally forbidden denominator value.

linkedPractice.prompt: Solve (x² − x − 2)/(x² − 6x + 8) ≤ 0. Explain why cancelling a common factor does not make every value of x valid. Give your final solution as intervals. [7 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.note: Horizontal scaling and x-axis reversal under f(-2x) must be checked graphically.

linkedPractice.prompt: Let f(x)=x³−3x and g(x)=f(−2x). Sketch y=g(x), labelling all three x-intercepts and both stationary points. Explain where the original points (−1,2) and (1,−2) move, and state the effect on the graph's horizontal scale and orientation. [7 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.note: Combined transformations: follow coordinates, roots and turning points.

linkedPractice.prompt: Let f(x)=x² and g(x)=−2f(2x+4)+1. Draw a sketch of y=g(x), showing its turning point, its line of symmetry, the images of the original points (−1,1) and (1,1), and both exact x-intercepts. Show how the input and output transformations act on coordinates. [6 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

linkedPractice.prompt: Let f(x)=x²−4x+1 and g(x)=−2f(1−2x)+3. (a) Complete the square for f. (b) Describe a valid ordered sequence of graph transformations giving y=g(x) from y=f(x). (c) Express g as a quadratic in x and find the turning point. (d) Find both exact x-intercepts of g. [9 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.note: Tangent geometry to circles, not only the memorised equation.

linkedPractice.prompt: A circle is given by x²+y²−4x−6y−12=0. (a) Find its centre and radius. (b) Verify that P=(5,7) lies on the circle. (c) Find an exact equation of the tangent to the circle at P. (d) Find both axis intercepts of this tangent. [7 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.originalSkill: Sine rule, cosine rule and triangle area
rows.note: Check both legitimate sine-rule branches of ambiguous triangle, not just one.

linkedPractice.prompt: In triangle ABC, sides a and b are opposite angles A and B respectively. A=30°, a=10 cm and b=14 cm. (a) Use the sine rule to find sin B. (b) Show that two different values of B are possible and calculate both. (c) For each triangle, calculate C and the opposite side c to 3 significant figures. (d) Explain why using only the inverse sine calculator output would miss a valid triangle. [8 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.note: Retrieve exponential-model constants from slope/intercept of log graph with domain and units.

linkedPractice.prompt: A quantity P is modelled by P=Ae^(−kt), where A>0 and k>0. A straight-line graph of ln P against t passes through (2, 1.5) and (7, 0.5). (a) Find k and ln A. (b) Write an exact expression for P in terms of t and give A to 3 significant figures. (c) Find the time when P=3, giving your answer to 3 decimal places. (d) Calculate the time for the model quantity to halve, and explain one limitation of using the graph to predict P at t=20. [8 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.originalSkill: Stationary points, maxima/minima and second derivative caveats
rows.note: Calculate domain, stationary points and justify an actual constrained maximum.

linkedPractice.prompt: A 20 cm by 12 cm rectangle of card has a square of side x cm cut from each corner. The edges are folded up to form an open-top box. (a) Show that its volume is V=4x³−64x²+240x, stating the possible values of x. (b) Find every stationary value of x and decide which is physically possible. (c) Find the maximum box volume to 3 significant figures, and justify that it is a maximum. [7 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.originalSkill: Definite integral versus unsigned total area
rows.note: Check signed definite integral separately from unsigned total area.

linkedPractice.prompt: For y=x²−5x+6 over 0≤x≤4, calculate (a) the signed definite integral from 0 to 4 and (b) the total area between the curve and the x-axis. You must show where the graph lies below the axis and split the integral correctly. Give exact answers. [8 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.note: Show matching scalar multiples or vector intersection reasoning, not only quote collinearity.

linkedPractice.prompt: A, B and C have position vectors (−1, 2), (3, 10) and (k, 20). Given that A, B and C are distinct and collinear, find k and the ratio AB:BC.
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

linkedPractice.prompt: Points A, B and C have position vectors (1,2), (7,−1) and (−2,8). P is the midpoint of BC and Q is the midpoint of AC. (a) Find the position vectors of P and Q. (b) Show by vector methods that the points on AP and BQ two-thirds of the way from A and B respectively coincide. (c) Give their common position vector and the ratio AG:GP. [8 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

rows.originalSkill: Vector internal division in a ratio
rows.note: Explicit internal division and position-vector ratios require full workings.

linkedPractice.prompt: A = (2, −5), B = (14, 7), C = (−1, 4). Point P divides AB internally in the ratio AP:PB = 1:3. Find P and the unit vector in the direction from C to P. Show your working.
linkedPractice.subject: Maths

linkedPractice.prompt: Points A, B and C have position vectors (1,2), (7,−1) and (−2,8). P is the midpoint of BC and Q is the midpoint of AC. (a) Find the position vectors of P and Q. (b) Show by vector methods that the points on AP and BQ two-thirds of the way from A and B respectively coincide. (c) Give their common position vector and the ratio AG:GP. [8 marks]
linkedPractice.subject: Maths
